title: How Leper Colonies Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain leprosy (Hansen's disease): its ancient origins, the Mycobacterium leprae bacterium and its nerve damage, biblical and medieval treatment of lepers, the rise of leper colonies and 'ugly laws', Hawaii's Kalaupapa leper colony and Father Damien, the Carville, Louisiana hospital and the development of drug cures, the persistence of stigma in India, and a listener email from Dan Garbon of SR-71 about one-hit-wonder life.

segments.title: Opening banter and the word 'unclean'
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about lepers having to call out 'unclean' and about the preferred term Hansen's disease.

segments.title: What leprosy is and how it spreads
segments.summary: Leprosy is an ancient bacterial infection that likely originated in Africa and infects only humans (and possibly armadillos). It is rare in the US, has a long incubation period, is curable, and is not very contagious; transmission is still not fully understood.

segments.title: How the bacterium damages the body
segments.summary: Mycobacterium leprae damages nerves, causing sores, muscle weakness, loss of pain sensation, amputations, and shortened fingers, by hijacking Schwann cells.

segments.title: Leprosy in the Bible and early segregation
segments.summary: The biblical word 'leprosy' covered many skin diseases; Leviticus required people with skin sores to live outside camp, an early form of segregation. Medieval towns pushed lepers to outskirts, and lepers were sometimes persecuted or killed.

segments.title: Ugly laws, Hawaii's exile law, and prison-like colonies
segments.summary: In the 19th century, Chicago passed an ugly law barring disfigured people from public places, and Hawaii made leprosy a crime in 1865, exiling patients to Kalaupapa. Colonies were run like prisons with no hope of release.

segments.title: Kalaupapa, Father Damien, and Carville
segments.summary: Kalaupapa on Molokai was founded in 1866 and was naturally isolated. Father Damien improved life there and advocated for patients; he died of leprosy and was canonized. Kalaupapa became a national park in 1980. The US opened a hospital at Carville, Louisiana, where drug treatments were developed.

segments.title: Stigma today and listener mail
segments.summary: Colonies closed from the 1960s on as cures emerged. Stigma persists in places like India, and an Ohio prisoner was treated for leprosy. The hosts close with listener mail from Dan Garbon of SR-71 about being a one-hit wonder.
